title: Growing Good King Henry
subtitle: An old English perennial potherb grown for its leaves, shoots, and flower spikes.
excerpt: Good King Henry is a hardy perennial grown for its spinach-like leaves in spring and early summer. It establishes slowly but persists for years in fertile soil with light shade tolerance, and the tender spring shoots are the best part of the harvest.
sourceNotes: Species information from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org) and Agroforestry Research Trust species data. UK cultivation notes from Garden Organic perennial vegetables guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant whose leaves or stems are cooked and eaten as a vegetable. Good King Henry, fat hen, and orache are traditional potherbs that were grown in kitchen gardens before spinach became the standard leaf crop.

content.text: Good King Henry is a traditional English

grown for its spring leaves and shoots. It was common in cottage gardens before spinach took over as the standard leaf crop. The young leaves are used like spinach; the flower spikes, cut while still tight, are cooked like asparagus.
It establishes slowly. The first season produces sparse leaves. From the second year the plant produces a reliable spring harvest from March to June before going to seed.

Good King Henry prefers fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade. It tolerates light shade better than most perennial vegetables. Avoid thin, dry, or very acid soils. It grows poorly on sand without regular watering.

Sow seed in pots in March or direct in April. Seed can be slow to germinate: soak overnight before sowing to improve germination. Plant out when the seedling has three or four leaves. Space plants 30 to 45 cm apart. Plants can also be divided in autumn once established.

From the second year, harvest young leaves from March onwards. Pick the outer leaves and leave the central growing tip intact. Cut the flower spikes when still in bud, before the flowers open: these are the most tender part. Stop harvesting in June and let the plant build root reserves through summer and autumn.

attrs.title: Oxalic acid
attrs.body: Like spinach, sorrel, and chard, Good King Henry contains oxalic acid. This is not a problem in small quantities, but avoid eating it raw in large amounts. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid content. People with kidney stones or gout are often advised to eat these vegetables only occasionally.
